results.title: Columbia House closure sparks nostalgia for a bygone music scam
results.author: Alex Galbraith
results.content:
Even if you aren’t old enough to remember the heyday of Columbia House, you’re probably familiar with the scam at its center. The mail-order club would offer customers eight to 12 CDs, tapes, records — and, in later years, DVDs and blu-rays — for a penny. By agreeing to the arrangement, users were signed up for a scheme where they agreed to purchase a certain number of products over a specific amount of time at full price. Each month, they were sent a mailer promoting the “Selection of the Month,” and if the customer failed to return the rejection form, Columbia House would send them the new release and charge their account.
The practice of requiring customers to opt-out or be charged is called negative-option billing, and it inspired no end of complaints from customers. Columbia House drew further claims of bad business by allegedly refusing to acknowledge payments, discounting items so that users’ purchases fell just below the agreed-upon threshold and being a notoriously difficult subscription to terminate.
That Columbia House was owned by massive record labels for much of its existence, and that the club manufactured their own cheaper versions of the releases to cut costs, gave the whole process an even more corrupt odor.
Columbia House was a bum deal for musicians as well, selling the CDs at a reduced price and offering the artists a smaller royalty percentage, the argument being that the cut paid for the mail-order club’s marketing. That Columbia House was owned by massive record labels for much of its existence, and that the club manufactured their own cheaper versions of the releases to cut costs, gave the whole process an even more corrupt odor. Pearl Jam protested the practices of Columbia House, and the bum deal it gave artists, but made little headway as the club boomed to 16 million members in the 1990s.
Given all that, I was somewhat surprised to see heartfelt eulogies for the mail-order racket when Columbia House announced it was ceasing operations later this year. Social media buzzed with stories about how “magical” it was to get CDs in far-flung locations. One academic who immigrated to the United States said junk mail from the retailer helped convince her that she’d really become an American. Others lamented the death of a “part of their childhood.”
Most of the rosy posts made some mention of the fact that Columbia House’s operation was unethical at best, but that the customer-service runarounds, unwelcome bills and general scuzziness had all faded with time. Where the company was once the best-known name in media rip-offs, it now leaves behind only mass-produced plastic and fuzzy memories.
Like Blockbuster, which was decried in its time as a killer of mom-and-pop video stores that ripped off customers with steep late fees, Columbia House died long after the average music consumer ceased doing business with it. That can account for at least some of the paeans to building a music collection on the cheap, or paying extortionate prices for movies once your skeevier dollar-video-shop was run out of town, but it’s far from the whole story. Awash in constant robot spam callers seeking sensitive information, in a country where the president is running his own cryptocurrency grift, the Columbia House swindle feels quaint.
In part, this is thanks to the technology at the heart of Columbia House. In an era before widespread tracking technology followed everyone’s consumption habits around the internet, Columbia House was remarkably easy to scam back. People signed up their pets, used aliases and played games with mailing addresses to bilk the company out of new releases for less than the cost of a penny. The ads, which came as paper mailers — in contrast to soon-to-be popular malware, pop-up ads and phishing emails — were decidedly less invasive and easily ignored. (After all, their easy-to-miss nature was a key part of the Columbia House business model.)
Start your day with essential news from Salon.
Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.
And unlike the bank-draining, generative AI-boosted rip-offs of 2026, you did actually get something for your trouble. Customers who forgot to send a postcard saying they wanted nothing to do with ‘90s Steven Tyler can still point to a copy of “Nine Lives” on their shelves. My own classic-rock-loving father ended up with copies of Whitney Houston and Alanis Morissette albums that he, left to his own devices, wouldn’t have sought out. But “Heartbreak Hotel” and “You Oughtta Know” were regularly spun in the car.
Nowadays, the taboo around scamming has fallen out of fashion with Gen Z, who see devious business models as a way to get ahead in a rigged economy. Amazon and other online marketplaces created a boom for drop-shippers to mark up products without providing any further value to customers. The internet-savvy and unscrupulous were quick to cash in. More than a decade after scam rap emerged from the buzzier, grimier corners of Detroit hip-hop, a scammer anthem from a South Floridian is arguably the song of the summer.
Americans lose more than $100 billion to scams every single year. As more and more of the country’s citizens feel like they’re being had, the Trump administration doesn’t seem to be rushing to stop the con. In fact, there’s plenty of evidence that they could be in on it.
White House insiders are reportedly using privileged information to place wagers on grey-area betting platforms. Nine accounts on the platform Polymarket made millions on U.S. military actions in Iran, winning nearly all of their 80 wagers on U.S. strikes and ceasefire negotiations. The former White House teleprompter operator allegedly made tens of thousands placing bets on what words Donald Trump might use in his speeches. The president himself has spent much of his second term accepting luxurious gifts and donations that sure read like bribes in the right light. Trump has increased his net worth by more than $2 billion in his second term, largely through the launch of a crypto firm operated by his sons. He accepted a $400 million jet from the royal family of Qatar and has pardoned multiple people after their families made large donations to his campaign. Former White House ethics czar Norm Eisen told the Washington Post that Trump had “fully monetize[d] the Oval Office” and was carrying out “corruption on a scale that . . . has few rivals in world history.”
What’s paying full price for an Ugly Kid Joe CD you never wanted compared to all that?

results.summary:
The mail-order music club Columbia House is closing its operations, prompting reflection on its controversial negative-option billing model and its legacy as a quintessential 20th-century consumer experience.

### Key Points
- Columbia House utilized negative-option billing, automatically shipping and charging customers for monthly selections unless they returned a rejection form.
- The company faced widespread criticism for difficult cancellation processes, disputed payments, and reduced royalty payouts to recording artists.
- At its peak in the 1990s, the club boasted 16 million members, often manufacturing its own lower-cost versions of popular albums and movies.
- Consumers frequently exploited the system by using aliases or signing up pets to receive discounted media, turning the scam back on the retailer.
- The business model is now viewed as a quaint predecessor to modern, high-stakes digital scams and sophisticated online marketplace exploitation.

### Why it Matters
The decline of Columbia House highlights a shift in how consumers perceive corporate exploitation in an era of increasingly complex digital fraud. While the club was once a symbol of predatory retail, its legacy is now being recontextualized against modern, large-scale political and financial corruption.

The recent surge in Bitcoin’s (CRYPTO: $BTC $MSTR
Bitcoin was trading at $77,300 U.S. early on Aug. 21, up 23% from $62,800 U.S. at the start of the week.

When Bitcoin hit its low for the year of $58,000 U.S. at the end of June, Strategy was sitting on an unrealized loss of $13 billion U.S.
The company sold nearly 7,000 Bitcoin at a loss in recent months as it sought to replenish its cash reserves and raise money to cover the dividend on its preferred stock (NASDAQ: $STRC
It remains to be seen what Strategy will do now that its back in the black on its Bitcoin holdings. At the current price of $77,300 U.S., Strategy’s BTC holdings are worth $64.97 billion U.S.

Bitcoin prices surged to $77,300 this week, returning major corporate holder Strategy to profitability with an unrealized gain of $1.4 billion on its massive cryptocurrency investment portfolio.

### Key Points
- Bitcoin rose 23% from $62,800 to $77,300 following U.S. Treasury bond market intervention and proposed Clarity Act legislation.
- Strategy currently holds 840,447 Bitcoin, valued at approximately $64.97 billion at the latest market price.
- The company’s average acquisition cost per Bitcoin is $75,385, placing its current holdings back into a profitable position.
- Strategy previously faced an unrealized loss of $13 billion when Bitcoin prices dropped to a yearly low of $58,000 in June.
- To manage cash reserves and preferred stock dividends, the firm sold nearly 7,000 Bitcoin at a loss earlier this year.

### Why it Matters
This recovery highlights the extreme volatility inherent in corporate cryptocurrency strategies and the significant impact of macroeconomic policy on digital asset valuations. As the largest corporate Bitcoin owner, Strategy’s return to profitability serves as a key indicator for institutional investors monitoring the long-term viability of holding crypto on a corporate balance sheet.

results.title: John Ternus as CEO could bring ‘bigger acquisitions,’ new product categories: analyst
results.author: Ryan Christoffel
results.content:
Tim Cook is in his final weeks as Apple CEO, with John Ternus set to take over the top job on September 1. And per Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan, Ternus could usher in a bolder, riskier era at Apple.
John Ternus expected to take more risks as CEO with new products, acquisitions, R&D
Apple’s CEO transition is almost complete. So far, the company has worked very hard to emphasize the continuity Ternus will bring to the role.
But not everyone at Wall Street seems to believe Ternus will follow Cook’s example as closely.
In a research note seen by The Street, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan reiterates a strong ‘Buy’ rating for Apple. And a key part of that endorsement relates to expectations that Ternus will maintain Cook’s legacy while also having a bigger “risk appetite.” Moz Farooque writes:
The bank underscored Apple’s move away from its net-cash-neutral objective as an early signal that its management might be more willing to deploy capital. That would translate into heavier R&D spending, more CapEx, and potentially bigger acquisitions, areas that weren’t major features of Cook’s strategy.
Under Ternus, BofA sees the possibility of Apple moving much more quickly into new categories, including AI glasses, camera-equipped AirPods, smart rings, home automation, personal assistants, and robotics.
Essentially, BofA believes Ternus will maintain Cook’s legacy of turning Apple into a highly profitable global machine. But he’s also expected to leverage the company’s position of strength to make riskier moves in the future.
We likely won’t see any major changes right when Ternus takes over as CEO. But perhaps in the months to come, any potential differing priorities will start to become clear.
What are you expecting from John Ternus as Apple’s CEO? Let us know in the comments.
results.summary:
John Ternus is set to succeed Tim Cook as Apple CEO on September 1, with analysts predicting a shift toward bolder product development and increased capital deployment strategies.

### Key Points
- John Ternus will officially assume the role of Apple CEO on September 1, succeeding long-time leader Tim Cook.
- Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan suggests the company may pivot toward a higher risk appetite regarding research and development.
- Apple is reportedly moving away from its net-cash-neutral objective to facilitate larger capital expenditures and potential acquisitions.
- Future product explorations may include AI-integrated glasses, smart rings, robotics, and advanced home automation technologies.
- Wall Street maintains a positive outlook on the transition, expecting Ternus to balance existing profitability with new market expansion.

### Why it Matters
This leadership transition signals a potential strategic evolution for one of the world's most valuable companies as it seeks new growth avenues beyond its core hardware lineup. Investors are closely watching whether this shift toward aggressive R&D and capital deployment will successfully diversify Apple's revenue streams in an increasingly competitive technology landscape.

results.content:
Imagine spending 35 years building the most recognizable booth at the world’s biggest consumer electronics show, then deciding one year to just… not. That is exactly what Samsung is doing at IFA 2026. The company is hosting its own event at the Humboldt Carré, a conference venue in central Berlin, eight kilometers from Messe, starting September 2, two days before the official show opens. Samsung frames this as a focused environment for media briefings, retail meetings, and product launches, following the same logic it applied at CES 2026 when it left the Las Vegas Convention Center for the Wynn Hotel. Doing it twice in the same year starts to look less like a pivot and more like a policy.
While Samsung manages its event across town, Xiaomi is inside Messe Berlin, confirmed for Hall 6.2, with a full ecosystem pitch and no obvious competitor stealing the spotlight. Xiaomi announced its IFA commitment at the official IFA Kick-Off on June 30, attaching a €7.4 billion AI R&D budget to the news, covering electric vehicles, robotics, and operating systems through 2028. Its IoT platform connects over 1.16 billion devices as of mid-2026, which gives the “Human x Car x Home” pitch real substance beyond the marketing copy. Samsung will sponsor the IFA Creator Hub, a content studio for influencers at Palais am Funkturm. But a sponsorship is a very different thing from anchoring a show floor, and Xiaomi is anchoring the show floor.
At CES 2026, Samsung left the Las Vegas Convention Center for the Wynn Hotel and applied museum-style layout techniques to give visitors more time with each product. The Humboldt Carré plan at IFA runs on exactly the same idea, consolidating launches, tech forums, and partner meetings under one roof with dedicated space for hands-on AI appliance experiences. Samsung also has a footprint inside Messe Berlin as the main sponsor of the IFA Creator Hub, a content studio for influencers at Palais am Funkturm. It will run its own programming there throughout show week. But sponsoring a content studio is a different brand position from anchoring a product booth, and on the Messe floor, that position now belongs to whoever occupies it.
Reports place the Galaxy S26 FE launch on September 4, the same day IFA officially opens, which means every journalist in Berlin will be writing about a Samsung phone from inside a building Samsung chose not to be in. LG, TCL, and Hisense all held their hall bookings and published their stand numbers months ago. Xiaomi is in Hall 6.2, a short walk from the main press areas. The reporters who glance up from S26 FE coverage will be standing next to Samsung’s biggest competitors. The brand generating the most ambient attention on the Messe floor will simply be the one that actually showed up.
Xiaomi’s pitch at IFA 2026 carries weight because the company has actually built the ecosystem it is selling. Its IoT platform connects over 1.16 billion devices as of June 2026, phones and laptops excluded, which gives the “Human x Car x Home” framing real shelf-stocking credibility for European retailers. The €7.4 billion AI R&D commitment for 2026 to 2028, spanning electric vehicles, robotics, and operating systems, is sized for institutional buyers rather than spec-sheet readers. Xiaomi landed on the Fortune Global 500 for the seventh consecutive year in July 2026, ranked 232nd. It arrives at IFA knowing exactly what it wants from a European room, and with the numbers to back that up.
Samsung’s controlled-environment strategy has a clean logic that gets harder to apply the bigger the show it leaves behind. Moving off the floor eliminates accidental comparisons, crowded aisles, and competitor booths visible from your own press conference, but it also removes the organic brand visibility a trade show generates just by being a trade show. Xiaomi does not have that problem this year. It is physically present in the room where buying decisions happen, where retail partnerships get formed over product demos, and where IFA’s roughly 220,000 annual visitors walk through looking for the next big thing. If the floor plan is the argument, Xiaomi is winning it before the doors even open.
results.summary:
Samsung is shifting its IFA 2026 presence to a private venue in Berlin, leaving its traditional trade show floor space to competitors like Xiaomi for the upcoming event.

### Key Points
- Samsung will host its product launches and media briefings at the Humboldt Carré starting September 2, rather than maintaining a traditional booth at Messe Berlin.
- Xiaomi has secured a prominent position in Hall 6.2 to showcase its "Human x Car x Home" ecosystem, supported by a €7.4 billion AI R&D budget.
- Samsung will remain involved at IFA 2026 as the primary sponsor of the IFA Creator Hub located at the Palais am Funkturm.
- The Galaxy S26 FE is expected to launch on September 4, coinciding with the official opening of the IFA trade show.
- Xiaomi’s IoT platform currently connects over 1.16 billion devices, excluding smartphones and laptops, as of mid-2026.

### Why it Matters
Samsung’s move to private venues reflects a growing trend among major tech firms to prioritize controlled environments over the chaotic, competitor-heavy atmosphere of traditional trade show floors. However, this strategy risks ceding organic brand visibility and direct retail engagement to rivals like Xiaomi, who are positioning themselves as the primary anchors for show attendees and industry buyers.

results.title: This iOS 27 Shortcut Stopped My Mindless Scrolling
results.author: Bridget Carey
results.content:
It got to the point where I couldn’t remember why I picked up my phone. I compulsively opened Threads and TikTok at all hours of the day and got sucked into the endless scroll — but I found a way to retrain my brain this week, thanks to a new iOS 27 feature.
I’m beta testing the upcoming operating system and its refreshed Shortcuts app, which lets you program your iPhone to do things using ordinary language. It’s called Describe a Shortcut. I speak my wishes into the app, and it obeys.
So in this week’s One More Thing video, which you can watch embedded above, I found out what happens when you tell Shortcuts to not let you open Instagram (or Threads, or TikTok) during work hours.
This is probably not what Apple developers had in mind for Shortcuts. After all, the Apple Screen Time app already has plenty of ways to help curb a social media addiction. But reprograming my phone to turn it into a brick is more fun than paying for another company to “Brick” my phone. (Yes, people do this.)
For more One More Thing, subscribe to our YouTube page to catch Bridget Carey breaking down the latest Apple news and issues every Friday.
results.summary:
Apple is testing a new "Describe a Shortcut" feature in the upcoming iOS 18 beta that allows users to program iPhone automation tasks using simple, natural language commands.

### Key Points
- The new "Describe a Shortcut" tool enables users to create custom iPhone automations by speaking instructions into the Shortcuts app.
- Beta testers are using the feature to restrict access to specific social media applications like Instagram, Threads, and TikTok during work hours.
- This functionality serves as an alternative to Apple’s existing Screen Time settings for managing digital habits and reducing screen addiction.
- The feature is part of the upcoming iOS operating system update currently being evaluated by developers and early testers.

### Why it Matters
This update simplifies complex automation tasks, making advanced iPhone customization accessible to users without technical programming skills. By allowing more granular control over app usage, Apple is providing a flexible tool that could significantly alter how users manage their daily digital consumption.

results.title: ‘Where’s the humanity?’ Why job seekers say hiring is ‘broken’
results.author: Rachel Barber, USA TODAY
results.content:
‘Where’s the humanity?’ Why job seekers say hiring is ‘broken’
After getting a layoff notice in May, engineer Todd Hendricks, 46, started his job search. One Friday, he signed on to Zoom for the coding round of a multistep interview process and waited for someone to appear. No one did.
He reached out to the recruiter and heard nothing back. The next Monday, an email landed in his inbox. The company said it was no longer moving forward with his application, based on his performance in the interview he says never happened.
Hendricks is one of many American job seekers who believe the hiring process is “broken.” Finding a job has rarely been easy, but in 2026, fierce competition, the growing use of artificial intelligence and a lack of trust in employers have further complicated the process.
U.S. employers added a historically low number of jobs in 2025. Hiring bounced back in the spring but has cooled in recent months. Employers shed 23,000 roles in July. People are still getting hired, though much of the recent job growth has been concentrated in a few select sectors, like health care. The search is tougher for candidates like Hendricks, who is looking for a job in technology – an industry that accounts for 31% of all job cuts announced this year, according to a Challenger, Gray & Christmas report.
The nation's unemployment rate was relatively low at 4.1% in July, though economists say it fell this year largely because workers dropped out of the labor force, not because a massive number of candidates were hired. Some analysts believe one reason behind the departures is burnout from the job search.
'Volume has replaced intention'
After being laid off in May 2023, Candee Petersen said she secured a new job three months later in August, only to be laid off again in September. Though she has landed some contract work since, Petersen, 54, said that about 5,000 applications later, she’s still without a full-time job. A former executive administrative business partner, she first applied to similar roles. As time dragged on, she applied to “everything” that aligned with her skill set.
Amanda Dobson, founder of Clear Pathways, an HR and leadership advisory firm, said one of the problems with hiring today may be that “volume has replaced intention” for job seekers and recruiters alike.
The explosion of remote work amid the COVID-19 pandemic led to more applicants vying for the same jobs around the country rather than competing with just those in their area or those willing to relocate for a position, Dobson said.
U.S. applicants per open role have doubled since spring 2022, according to LinkedIn research released at the start of this year. It found that 65% of people said finding a job had become more challenging, citing competition as the main obstacle.
Recruiters used to review about 100 applications per role in early 2021. They are now processing 291 per hire, according to a 2026 Talent Trends report by Ashby, a recruiting platform.
Employers receive hundreds of applications and cannot respond to each. Applicants don’t hear back, so they apply for more jobs, and the cycle continues, Dobson said.
Vicki Salemi, a career expert at job listings site Monster, said she has seen lifeguards apply to certified public accountant roles and a candidate apply to 10 positions at the same company at one time, a “red flag” to the employer. She and Dobson advise job seekers to narrow their search.
If you’re “sending out 500 applications as a candidate, there’s no way that you actually want to work for those 500 jobs,” Dobson said. “Instead of spending the energy – the five to 10 minutes per application that you’re sending out – and sending it out 500 times, take 20 minutes on your resume and take 20 minutes on your application to thoughtfully answer the application questions.”
'Where's the humanity' in the AI age?
A problem with that approach may be that only 10% of job seekers feel that most of their applications are reviewed by a human, according to LiveCareer’s 2025 Job Search Frustration Survey, though 64% believed their resumes were optimized for applicant tracking systems.
Dobson said they’re right to be skeptical.
“I talk with a lot of HR professionals, and in the recruitment process, they’re not looking at every single resume,” she said. “They’re letting the systems do that.”
At 93%, most recruiters surveyed by LinkedIn late last year said they planned to increase their AI use in 2026, and 59% said the technology was already helping them discover new candidates. Some have gone so far as to introduce AI interviewers.
“Nobody talks to you anymore. You get invitations, ‘Oh, we have an AI interview.' I’m not talking to AI. I’m not sending a Loom video just so you can see me sitting there talking to myself,” Petersen said. “Where’s the humanity in this?”
But applicants are using AI, too. The LinkedIn survey found 81% of people had used AI to assist their job search or said they planned to. Hendricks described it as an “automation arms race.”
“Applicants are increasingly using AI to tailor their resumes and cover letters on the applications, and employers increasingly will use AI or other automated systems to filter and rank those applications,” he said.
Hendricks is not relying on AI to rewrite his applications, however.
“Even before AI, there was this concept that you should have a unique resume for every job application,” he said. “Now, AI has made that easier, whereas people used to do it by hand. But I mean, my experience is my experience. I’m not going to augment it in ways that aren’t true.”
Even if an applicant uses AI to help optimize their application, if a tracking system is flagging resumes for specific keywords or phrases, a misplaced comma may be the reason an applicant is never seriously considered, Dobson said.
“Because of where a comma was placed in their criteria, they were auto-rejecting a lot of candidates that they should have been reviewing,” she said of one company. “We’re relying too heavily on these systems and not using a human to review candidates.”
'Ghost jobs' and a lack of trust
The usual way people measure job market tightness is by comparing the number of open jobs with the number of unemployed people.
However, “a large and rising share of job postings target already-employed workers or represent inactive listings,” a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis analysis said last November. “As a result, the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio now overstates how tight the labor market truly is for unemployed workers.”
Even if a job listing is not a scam, a company may post a role while planning to hire internally or recruiting someone already employed elsewhere. A budget change could mean a role that was once real is now cut. In those cases, a company may advertise an opening that job seekers never had a realistic chance of getting. Candidates call these listings “ghost jobs.”
Another Ashby report released last year analyzing data from its customer base found that 82% of open jobs in 2024 led to a real hire but that 5.5% were paused, 1% led to an offer but no hire, and 3.5% were pulled without a reason given.
Applicants “have no way to know whether another candidate was selected, or the hiring plan changed, or the position was never actively being filled, and it was just a listing to increase the appearance of success on the part of the company,” Hendricks said. “If I apply to 10 positions and receive no interviews, I need to know whether that means I’m targeting the wrong roles, or I’m presenting my experience poorly, or I’m applying to positions that weren't realistic opportunities in the first place.”
Salemi said that while it’s true there are job postings unemployed candidates never had a realistic chance of getting, companies "don’t post them just for fun” but rather to build a talent pipeline or stack of resumes to reference the next time they have an opening.
Talent pipelines haven’t worked out for Petersen.
“Nobody ever has called me back because they built a pipeline from a job that I applied to three years ago,” Petersen said.
Doubting job descriptions and scanning for scams
Candidates have more trust in job postings when companies share clear salary ranges as well as transparent expectations around workload and hours, a new Monster report found. But they don’t always get them.
After reviewing enough job posts that listed the position as remote only to find out the company requires employees to work in office, Petersen doesn’t trust job descriptions anymore.
She’s not alone. Only 10% of workers say job descriptions “always” accurately reflect the reality of the role, according to the Monster report. It found that 81% of workers surveyed said they at least sometimes encounter job descriptions that “feel vague or overly polished.”
Beyond determining whether a company means what it says in a job posting, candidates also are navigating scam offers. Petersen said she receives suspicious texts and emails promising to help her land a job “every day.”
“You get, ‘Of course. Yeah. We have a job for you, but you need to pay this person to rewrite your resume,’” she said. “It’s scary to see how many people will try to take advantage of somebody who’s already down.”
At 95%, most job seekers have encountered a suspicious job offer, and 98% said today's job market increases vulnerability to scams, a separate Monster report found.
To verify whether an opportunity is real, Salemi said, job seekers should ask themselves a few questions: Is it realistic? Does it highlight specific responsibilities? Is it listed on the company website? Does the company have a mailing address? Does the recruiter have a professional email address?
She reminds job seekers that most companies won’t need their Social Security number or address until after they are onboarded.
“Legitimate employers will not just immediately hire you without having screened you,” Salemi said. “Your gut was likely going to be right anyway. So trust it.”
Reach Rachel Barber at rbarber@usatoday.com, follow her on X @rachelbarber_, and subscribe to her newsletter "Making More of Your Money" here
results.summary:
American job seekers are facing an increasingly difficult hiring landscape defined by intense competition, widespread use of automated screening tools, and a growing prevalence of inactive job listings.

### Key Points
- U.S. employers are processing an average of 291 applications per hire, nearly triple the volume seen in early 2021.
- Technology sector roles account for 31% of all announced job cuts in 2026, contributing to a highly competitive market for engineers.
- Approximately 93% of recruiters plan to increase their use of artificial intelligence in 2026 to filter and rank candidate applications.
- Research indicates that a significant portion of online job postings are "ghost jobs," which are either inactive, paused, or intended only for internal candidates.
- Only 10% of job seekers believe their applications are reviewed by a human, leading to widespread frustration and a lack of trust in employers.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward automated, high-volume hiring processes has created an "automation arms race" that often alienates qualified candidates and obscures real employment opportunities. This disconnect forces job seekers to navigate a landscape where transparency is low and the risk of encountering scams or ghost listings is significantly elevated.

results.title: Nintendo Wipes Out 400+ Switch Emulator Repos in Single-Day GitHub Sweep
results.author: Ernesto Van der Sar
results.content:
GitHub is home to hundreds of millions of code repositories, including some repositories that rightsholders would rather not see online.
For Nintendo, Switch emulators have become the main challenge, one that keeps rearing its head.
Most of these emulators were killed off long ago. Yuzu settled in February 2024, for example, Ryujinx shut down that October, and the successors that tried to keep edited versions online have been targeted in waves ever since.
These waves keep coming. Earlier this week, Nintendo filed seven separate DMCA anti-circumvention notices at GitHub, all on the same day, targeting a variety of Switch emulator repositories and their forks. The combined reach is substantial. In the seven notices, more than 400 repositories were targeted.
More Than 400 Repos
The most detailed notice targets suyu, an emulator that became popular after Yuzu’s collapse. Because the reported network was larger than 100 repositories, GitHub processed the notice against the entire network, which covered 311 repos.
The remaining six notices ranged from a lone repository to networks of a few dozen, including the independent Skyline emulator, as shown below.
| Parent repo (notice) | Project | Targets | 
|---|---|---|
| vstyler96/suyu | suyu (yuzu successor) | 311 repos (full network) | 
| skyline-emu/skyline | Skyline (Android, independent) | 29 repos (full network) | 
| NicolasArvani/yuzu | yuzu fork | 14 repos (full network) | 
| liushuyu/yuzu-android | yuzu (Android port) | 8 repos (full network) | 
| exverge-0/yuzu-EA4176 | yuzu (Early Access build 4176) | 21 forks listed | 
| irlbunny-archive/MonoNX | MonoNX (C#-based) | 17 forks listed | 
| IpwnedU/yuzu-master | yuzu fork | Parent only | 
For four of the seven notices, the table shows GitHub’s own count of the processed network, including the parent repo. For the other three, no network details were published, so the table shows the repositories named in the notice itself, including some that were redacted as “[private].”
The legal argument is the same in all seven. Nintendo argues that the emulators exist to bypass the encryption that protects its games, which violates the DMCA.
“During operation, the emulators at the reported repositories necessarily use unauthorized copies of these cryptographic keys to decrypt unauthorized copies of Nintendo Switch games, or ROMs, at or immediately before runtime without Nintendo’s authorization,” the notice read.
Most of these repositories now link to notices informing visitors that they were removed. In some cases, they point to a 404 error, suggesting that the developer voluntarily removed the repository after being notified.
Precedents Without a Trial
To back the circumvention argument, every notice cites two court decisions as precedents, neither of which was challenged in court.
The first is the 2024 consent judgment against Tropic Haze, the company behind Yuzu, which ended in a $2.4 million settlement. The second is newer: Nintendo’s case against streamer Jesse Keighin, aka “EveryGameGuru,” who was ordered to pay $17,500 last October after a Colorado court entered a default judgment against him.
One was a settlement, the other a default judgment after Keighin reportedly stopped responding and destroyed evidence. In neither case did a court weigh the emulator circumvention question on the merits.
At the takedown stage Nintendo does not need to show a legal precedent. GitHub says it reviews circumvention claims carefully and will “err on the side of the developer, and leave the content up” when validity is unclear. The Yuzu framework has made Nintendo’s notices close to routine anyway.
Defunct Skyline & Future Horizon
Among the targeted emulators Skyline stands out, as it was a Switch emulator for Android devices, not a yuzu fork. Skyline’s developers shut the project down voluntarily in 2023, but as is often the case, the open source code survived.
This week, Nintendo’s takedown notice cleared a network of 29 Skyline repos, including code that has been dormant for years. This doesn’t necessarily deal with the problem permanently, as future takedown efforts are likely on the horizon.
Every emulator on this week’s list was already supposed to be gone. However, they were forked, mirrored, or revived, which put them on Nintendo’s radar again.
For Nintendo, getting these emulator repos removed from GitHub is the easy part. Keeping the code offline is a bigger challenge, as forks may reappear faster than the notices can remove them.
results.summary:
Nintendo has filed seven DMCA anti-circumvention notices with GitHub, resulting in the removal of over 400 repositories associated with various Nintendo Switch emulators and their community-maintained forks.

### Key Points
- Nintendo targeted over 400 repositories, including the popular Yuzu successor "suyu" and the Android-based Skyline emulator.
- The legal notices argue that these emulators violate the DMCA by bypassing cryptographic protections required to run unauthorized Nintendo Switch game files.
- GitHub processed the takedowns by removing entire networks of repositories, including dormant projects and independent forks.
- Nintendo cited the 2024 Tropic Haze settlement and a recent default judgment against streamer Jesse Keighin as legal precedents for their enforcement actions.
- Many affected repositories now display removal notices or 404 errors, though the open-source nature of the code allows for potential future redistribution.

### Why it Matters
These mass takedowns demonstrate Nintendo's aggressive strategy to curb software piracy by systematically removing emulator source code from major hosting platforms. While these actions effectively clear GitHub of current projects, the ease of forking open-source code suggests that developers may continue to revive or mirror these tools, creating an ongoing cycle of enforcement.

results.title: How To Build The Niche Skills Employers Actually Want
results.author:
Colleen Batchelder, Contributor, 
 Colleen Batchelder, Contributor
 https://www.forbes.com/sites/colleenbatchelder/
results.content:
Fewer than 50% of college students have even heard of the term "skills-based hiring," according to NACE's 2026 Student Survey of more than 17,000 students across 258 colleges. There’s a disconnect between recruiters and young job seekers. That's why applicants who understand what specific skills employees are screening for have an absolute advantage over their competition. Those niche skills help you stand out above the rest because they close the cracks and crevices of company needs.
Employers aren’t looking for vague, outdated keywords like "hard-working." They want you to bring more to the table.
What Are Niche Skills And Why Do Employers Value Them?
A niche skill is usually tied to one to two tasks, and tells someone what you are capable of, rather than providing a description. It’s not a personality trait, and it’s not necessarily tied to your degree.
General skills are on every resume. Everyone writes communication and teamwork. Transferable skills move between different roles, such as project management to content writing. But niche skills are much narrower, which is why only a fraction of people can actually claim them.
As AI absorbs more mundane tasks, niche skills become more valuable in 2026. In fact, according to Upwork, the demand for skills referencing AI grew to 109% year-over-year. And get this: 45% of business leaders said that they would pay a higher price for creativity and 47% for innovation. This is what employers are looking for, specific skills that can address these areas.
Employers still need human ingenuity and judgment, too. And those skills are harder to automate and replicate with AI, which is why the demand for people who have niche skills keeps increasing. This is why it’s one of the best forms of job security right now.
The Niche Skills Recruiters Are Looking For
A niche skill is an asset that can help you get hired because it can make you stand out in a competitive job market. It can also give you something tangible that you can use as leverage on salary and title because a named skill has true market value.
Pick one or two technical skills and then one that’s specifically operational. So, think of the list below as a buffet. Skills can also be refined further through overlap.
You just need to fill your plate with the skills that fit you best. The median salary ranges below come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The reports below support the demand section. If you want to go beyond the 20 skills, then feel free to look further into these reports:
- LinkedIn Skills on the Rise 2026
- Indeed Hiring Lab
- Upwork's Research Institute
- Coursera’s Job Skills Report 2026
1. AI Business Strategy
This skill requires you to figure out where AI actually belongs in a business and where it doesn’t. There are plenty of people who know how to use AI tools, but few who are selective about which ones are worth investing in.
- Industries hiring: Consulting firms, financial services, retail and healthcare.
- Typical roles: Strategy associate, business analyst and transformation associate.
- Salary range: $60,640 to $171,640 for management analysts.
- Demand: LinkedIn named AI business strategy as a rising skill category as companies evolve and integrate AI into products and processes.
- Who this fits: Business or economics graduates looking for a path that's not entirely technical.
2. Data Quality
This means having the ability to judge whether a data set can be trusted. As artificial intelligence becomes the new norm of most businesses, the ability to analyze is still necessary. After all, someone still has to vouch for the AI output quality.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, finance, retail and government.
- Typical roles: Data analyst, quality analyst and operations associate.
- Salary range: $67,240 to $199,130 for data scientists.
- Demand: Coursera recorded 108% year-over-year enrollment growth for this skill among data learners.
- Who this fits: Anyone comfortable working with spreadsheets.
3. Debugging
Your main job is to find out why something is broken and fix it. You work alongside AI coding, and you fix what it missed.
- Industries hiring: Software, financial, healthcare and government.
- Typical roles: Quality assurance (QA) analyst, software tester and technical support.
- Salary range: $61,440 to $167,010 for software quality assurance analysts and testers.
- Demand: As AI code becomes more prevalent, you need someone who can catch what it gets wrong and make it right.
- Who this fits: Anyone who has a coding background and knows how to spot errors within AI.
4. SQL
This skill requires you to understand the type of language that you need to communicate with a database.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, finance, retail, government and logistics.
- Typical roles: Data analyst, database administrator or business intelligence associate.
- Salary range: $60,230 to $163,320 for database administrators.
- Demand: SQL has a long shelf-life compared to other data tools. It’s been a foundational technology for 50 years and it’s still necessary today.
- Who this fits: Anyone who wants quick skills they can add to their resume.
5. AI Chatbot Development
This skill requires you to build conversational tools that handle support, internal questions and sales.
- Industries hiring: SaaS, e-commerce, financial services and healthcare.
- Typical roles: Software developer, AI developer and automation specialist.
- Salary range: $82,460 to $214,670 for software developers.
- Demand: Upwork recorded 71% year-over-year growth for AI chatbot development.
- Who this fits: Junior developers looking to step into a field that isn't overcrowded yet.
6. Web And Interface Design
This skill gives you the ability to design how a user interacts with the business’ website, app and digital presence. AI might provide dynamic templates for design, but it can't replicate human ingenuity when it comes to creating something user-friendly.
- Industries hiring: SaaS, e-commerce, media, healthcare and technology.
- Typical roles: UX designer, product designer and front-end designer.
- Salary range: $53,750 to $201,550 for web and digital interface designers.
- Demand: As artificial intelligence generates more web templates and copy and paste designs, the ability to know what sells and grabs the viewers becomes the difference-maker.
- Who this fits: Visual and creative thinkers who want a high-yielding salary without a computer science degree.
7. Content Creation
Everyone has the ability to produce tons of content now, but the niche skill that’s worth knowing is what to talk about, how to portray it and why it matters to your readers/viewers. Your main purpose is to create great copy, produce videos and design visuals that grab attention and translate to views.
- Industries hiring: Marketing, education, non-profits and media
- Typical roles: Copywriter, communications associate and content strategist.
- Salary range: $44,310 to $139,870 for writers and authors.
- Demand: With AI making content production easier, the ability to make it stand out becomes a top skill.
- Who this fits: Strong story-tellers who can bring things to life through writing or video content.
8. Governance, Risk Management And Compliance
This skill gives you the ability to manage for security and compliance with documentation so that the company can not only survive but feel confident if audited.
- Industries hiring: Banking, insurance, healthcare, government and energy.
- Typical roles: Risk analyst, audit associate and compliance associate.
- Salary range: $48,220 to $133,720 for compliance officers.
- Demand: LinkedIn named this skill as a rising category, especially as regulatory and security environments keep evolving.
- Who this fits: Anyone with an educational background in policy, pre-law or public health.
9. Employee Engagement And People Management
The main purpose of the skill is to keep the team functioning like a well-oiled machine, and it doesn't always have to be tied to the HR department.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, hospitality and retail.
- Typical roles: HR specialist, operations coordinator and team lead.
- Salary range: $47,180 to $128,720 for human resources specialists.
- Demand: Indeed found that HR skills are in demand in 27.3% of all job postings within the United States.
- Who this fits: Anyone who manages a team within any department at any level.
10. Talent Development And Mentorship
This skill shows you how to take someone from point A to point B and make them shine.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, technology, education and manufacturing.
- Typical roles: Training coordinator, onboarding specialist and learning and development associate.
- Salary range: $38,760 to $123,250 for training and development specialists.
- Demand: Onboarding new employees is expensive. If you’re good at talent development and mentorship, you can save your company time, energy, and money.
- Who this fits: Anyone who knows how to inspire people and enjoys coaching them along the journey.
11. Business Project Management
This skill means that you have the ability to run a project well and meet a deadline. It usually means that you can stay under budget and be organized during the process.
- Industries hiring: Construction, technology, consulting and healthcare.
- Typical roles: Project management specialist, program associate and project coordinator.
- Salary range: $61,580 to $167,970 for project management specialists.
- Demand: Every company functions under deadlines. Having someone who gets everyone on the same page is priceless.
- Who this fits: Anyone who enjoys organizing events, leading groups or running a club with ease.
12. Administrative And Calendar Management
This skill requires you to oversee office systems, the entire calendar and usually organizational structure. It sounds basic, but someone with this ability needs to be able to juggle a lot simultaneously.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, education, finance, legal services and most everywhere else.
- Typical roles: Executive assistant, office coordinator and operations associate.
- Salary range: $50,560 to $109,850 for executive secretaries and executive administrative assistants.
- Demand: Every profession needs someone who's organized and can keep things running smoothly. That stability builds morale and secures the bottom line.
- Who this fits: Anyone who finds spreadsheets, objectives and quarterly goals a fun pastime.
13. Supply Chain And Logistics Project Management
This skill means that you understand how the goods and services of your company move. You see the whole entire process, and you make sure that it's seamless.
- Industries hiring: Logistics, retail, e-commerce and manufacturing
- Typical roles: Logistics coordinator, supply chain associate and operations analyst.
- Salary range: $50,890 to $133,160 for logisticians.
- Demand: Whether it's a digital or physical product, most businesses need someone who can spot problems in the supply chain before they turn into permanent damage.
- Who this fits: Anyone who enjoys overseeing operations without needing to spend years in college for a business degree.
14. Medical Virtual Assistance
This skill requires you to handle day-to-day scheduling, medical records and patient coordination for a healthcare practice. Many times, it’s entirely remote. Now this skill has been impacted by AI. Many software programs enable transcription and voice-to-text options. However, someone is still needed to connect those systems to actual patients, and they need to catch what AI often misses.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, telehealth, insurance and medical billing.
- Typical roles: Medical administrative assistant, scheduler and patient coordinator.
- Salary range: $35,930 to $60,530 for medical secretaries and administrative assistants.
- Demand: Healthcare is always going to be an in-demand field, and paperwork is a big part of that. Someone is always going to be needed to interpret the system.
- Who this fits: Anyone who wants to work in the health care field remotely without needing further education.
15. Go-To-Market Strategy
This skill means that you know how to take a product and connect it to the buyer. You're good at messaging, funnels and understanding metrics.
- Industries hiring: SaaS, consumer products and e-commerce.
- Typical roles: Product marketing associate, market research analyst, and growth associate.
- Salary range: $43,390 to $155,480 for market research analysts and marketing specialists.
- Demand: LinkedIn named this skill as a rising skill category, especially as companies venture into new markets and marketing channels.
- Who this fits: Marketing or business graduates who want to fast-track past the internship tier.
16. Business Development
This skill is the ability to network, find common ground and build relationships for the purpose of revenue. Think of it like sales, but for the long term.
- Industries hiring: Professional services, real estate and SaaS.
- Typical roles: Business development representative, account associate and partnership associate.
- Salary range: $37,980 to $148,840 for sales representatives of services.
- Demand: In a world where people are tired of being pitched, the ability to build trust with the client before asking for anything in return is vital.
- Who this fits: Candidates who are great communicators, good listeners and know how to connect the dots.
17. Social Media Strategy
This skill is the ability to figure out what gets posted on what platform and the reason why. It's creating a gameplan that funnels in business, brand awareness and builds trust.
- Industries hiring: Consumer brands, non-profits and hospitality
- Typical roles: Social media coordinator, content strategist and public relations specialist.
- Salary range: $44,110 to $135,150 for PR specialists.
- Demand: Upwork recorded 36% year-over-year growth for social media strategy, and it's the fastest-growing sales and marketing skill of 2026.
- Who this fits: Creatives who are able to take trending topics and connect them to company goals.
18. Display Advertising
This skill is the ability to create and place advertisements in such a way that builds business. It requires you to understand metrics and how to get results.
- Industries hiring: Agencies, consumer brands, media and e-commerce.
- Typical roles: Media buyer, advertising sales agent and advertising coordinator.
- Salary range: $35,240 to $146,010 for advertising sales agents.
- Demand: Upwork labeled this as one of the top three fastest growing skills within sales and marketing in 2026.
- Who this fits: Anyone who's well-versed in marketing and metrics.
19. Video Editing
The skill is about piecing together video footage to create something concise and grabbing for viewers.
- Industries hiring: Media, education, consumer brands and marketing.
- Typical roles: Video editor, multimedia associate and content producer.
- Salary range: $40,280 to $148,550 for film and video editors.
- Demand: Upwork found that this skill was highly in demand in 2026, even as AI editing tools became more common and accessible.
- Who this fits: Anyone who likes focusing on the big picture and using TikTok, YouTube and Instagram.
20. Workplace Language Proficiency
This skill is about being bilingual and communicating effectively in the language of your field.
- Industries hiring: Healthcare, hospitality and logistics.
- Typical roles: Patient coordinator, bilingual operations associate and case manager.
- Salary range: $37,070 to $103,660 for interpreters and translators.
- Demand: Indeed found bilingual proficiency was an in-demand skill, especially in states like California, Massachusetts, Washington, Texas, Nevada and North Dakota.
- Who this fits: Anyone who speaks multiple languages and can easily break down complex topics within their field.
What It Takes To Develop Niche Skills
Building a niche skill doesn’t require another degree. You can build the skill through a certification or a YouTube tutorial.
The goal isn’t to attain more credentials, though. Niche skills show potential employers that you can build something: the social media calendar, the video reel or the spreadsheet. Companies want human ingenuity and expertise they can see in real time.
Now, you won’t become an expert overnight. Realistically, it takes a few weeks to months to build credibility and confidence in niche skills. But in time, your skills will impress the recruiter and get you to the next stages of the interview.
How To Showcase Your Niche Skills
Employers want proof. And matching the keywords in the job posting to your niche skills should be your first step. Put these skills in your resume, cover letter even your LinkedIn headline. During the interview, prove your skills with an actual artifact.
If you really want to stand out, prove it on video. Build evidence with an Instagram educational reel. As of 2025, content from professional Instagram accounts is now visible on Google. This means that what you post from a professional account is proof of your skillset. Employers can search your name and see your reel before you even step into the interview stage, and that definitely helps you stand out.
Always remember: narrow beats broad skills every time. Recruiters are actively looking to hire people with specific skill sets. Showcase them online, and use those keywords throughout your resume, cover letter and LinkedIn headline. You'll build proof and stand out to recruiters.

results.title: Republican Donors Fume Over Trump Putting Texas Senate Seat at Risk
results.author: Hafiz Rashid
results.content:
President Trump isn’t spending any campaign cash on close midterm election races, irking his fellow Republicans and putting contests like the Texas Senate seat in jeopardy.
In July, Politico reports, Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC didn’t spend any of its $400 million in the bank on Republican candidates, not even Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who only narrowly won his state’s GOP Senate primary and faces surging Democrat James Talarico.
Republican donors say that Trump needs to step up to keep the Lone Star State from sending its first Democrat to the Senate since 1993, considering that he endorsed scandal-ridden Paxton at the last minute over incumbent John Cornyn. That endorsement was probably the deciding factor in the close runoff election and now Paxton is polling just one point ahead of Talarico, unheard of in staunchly red Texas.
“The message to Trumpworld is, ‘you broke it, now you own it. You gotta spend some of your money to defend him because we’ve got bigger fish to fry,’” one GOP donor told Politico.
A second donor told the publication that “the general view is that’s Trump’s responsibility to bankroll, especially since Paxton took out one [of] the GOP Senate’s best fundraisers and is currently running a lackadaisical campaign.”
These donors would prefer to spend their money on open Senate races in Michigan and North Carolina, kicking out Democrats like Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and protecting vulnerable Republican Senate incumbents like Susan Collins in Maine and Dan Sullivan in Alaska.
“There’s a lot of people that, one, don’t really like Paxton at all, they think he’d be a terrible senator or they were loyal to Cornyn—or both,” a third GOP donor said to Politico. “This is a situation that we didn’t need to spend this money at all. We need it in North Carolina, in Georgia. To make Texas a toss-up is just a foolish, foolish decision.”
The National Republican Senatorial Committee is also staying out of Texas, preferring for now to spend its money on eight other races, making Trump’s unwillingness to open his coffers all the more glaring. While the NRSC plans to help set up a joint fundraising campaign with Paxton, any money above a certain amount would go back to the committee, according to Politico.
Trump has not spent any of his campaign money on a candidate since March, and the candidates he endorses keep losing. He’s refusing to accept any blame for Republicans becoming more and more unpopular, either. It seems like he cares less about his party controlling Congress than he does about his own pet projects.

Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC is facing criticism from Republican donors for withholding financial support from competitive midterm candidates, including Texas Senate hopeful Ken Paxton.

### Key Points
- The MAGA Inc. super PAC holds approximately $400 million but has not spent campaign funds on Republican candidates since March.
- Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is polling only one point ahead of Democrat James Talarico in a traditionally safe Republican state.
- Donors argue that Trump’s endorsement of Paxton in the primary necessitates his financial involvement in the current general election.
- The National Republican Senatorial Committee is prioritizing eight other competitive races over the Texas Senate contest.
- GOP donors prefer to allocate resources toward Senate races in states like Georgia, Michigan, and North Carolina.

### Why it Matters
The lack of financial support from Trump’s PAC threatens Republican control of the Senate by forcing the party to defend seats that are typically considered safe. This tension highlights a growing divide between the former president’s political priorities and the strategic goals of traditional GOP donors and committees.

results.title: US futures edge higher ahead of PMI data as Iran sanctions and oil remain in focus: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
results.author: Fiona Craig
results.content:
© Roberto Júnior
US stock futures moved modestly higher on Friday as investors awaited fresh business activity data while continuing to assess renewed pressure in bond markets, corporate earnings and Washington’s plans to impose sweeping sanctions on Iran.
Discount retailer Ross Stores (NASDAQ:ROST) was also in focus after raising its full-year earnings guidance following stronger-than-expected second-quarter results.
Wall Street futures pointed to a slightly firmer open after rising government bond yields weighed on equities during the previous session.
By 03:11 ET (07:11 GMT), Dow futures were up 65 points, or 0.1%, while S&P 500 futures gained 14 points, or 0.2%. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 115 points, equivalent to 0.4%.
US equities had finished lower on Thursday as sovereign bond yields resumed their climb following a sharp decline earlier in the week.
The US Treasury Department had provided temporary relief on Wednesday by announcing plans to increase purchases of longer-dated government debt. The move initially calmed concerns after the 30-year Treasury yield approached its highest level in almost two decades.
However, the bond rally quickly lost momentum.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge said comments from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent during a CNBC interview failed to provide lasting reassurance and were potentially “counterproductive by conveying both panic and powerlessness” in the face of broader pressures pushing yields higher.
Those pressures include the energy shock associated with the Iran conflict, expanding US fiscal deficits and rapidly increasing spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Investor sentiment was also affected by disappointing results from Walmart, according to Vital Knowledge.
A series of underwhelming earnings reports from retailers this week has increased scrutiny of the health of American consumers, particularly as households continue to contend with elevated living costs.
Investors are watching the sector closely for signs that inflation and higher borrowing costs are beginning to have a more significant impact on discretionary spending.
Markets will receive preliminary August US business activity figures on Friday, providing another indication of how the economy is coping with higher oil prices and changing expectations for monetary policy.
Business activity has so far remained relatively resilient despite the energy price shock generated by the Iran conflict and growing speculation that central banks may need to raise interest rates to contain inflation.
Deutsche Bank analysts noted that the US composite purchasing managers’ index, covering both manufacturing and services, reached its highest level of the year in July.
For August, S&P Global’s US services PMI is expected to ease slightly to 53.9, while the manufacturing PMI is forecast to rise to 54.0. Readings above 50 indicate an expansion in activity.
Ross Stores (NASDAQ:ROST) shares jumped more than 8% in extended trading after the discount retailer raised its annual profit outlook and reported second-quarter earnings ahead of market expectations.
Alongside rivals Burlington and TJX, as well as online competitors such as Shein and Amazon, Ross has been expanding its value-focused merchandise as consumers seek cheaper alternatives amid concerns about higher living costs.
CEO Jim Conroy told investors that customer spending had strengthened across merchandise categories and geographic regions, with particularly strong demand in the company’s home and cosmetics businesses.
Ross now expects annual earnings per share of between $8.61 and $8.77, substantially above its previous forecast of $7.50 to $7.74.
Adjusted earnings for the latest quarter reached $2.06 per share, exceeding expectations of $1.94, according to LSEG estimates cited by Reuters.
Geopolitical developments remained another major focus after Bessent said Washington was preparing severe new sanctions against Iran, reinforcing President Donald Trump’s threat to wage economic warfare against Tehran.
“It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC, adding that he will hold a press conference on Monday to outline the details of the plan.
The Treasury Secretary also urged China to cooperate with the sanctions programme, although Beijing has largely criticised proposals for additional restrictions against Iran.
Bessent’s remarks followed Trump’s warning on Wednesday that Iran faced “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale,” with the president arguing that months of US military and economic pressure had significantly weakened Tehran.
Iran rejected the threats, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing Trump of attempting to distract attention from domestic US issues, particularly the country’s rising debt burden.
Oil prices moved slightly lower following Bessent’s comments, retreating from one-month highs while remaining elevated as the confrontation between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz showed little sign of resolution.
Brent crude futures fell 0.4% to $93.41 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate futures declined 0.6% to $86.36.
Despite Friday’s pullback, Brent remained on course for a weekly increase of more than 5%, which would mark a second consecutive week of strong gains.
With the outlook for the Strait of Hormuz unresolved, energy prices, bond yields and the implications for inflation are likely to remain central considerations for investors alongside Friday’s US PMI figures.

results.title: From design to peel-ready sticker in a single go, the Liene PixCut S1 all-in-one printer and cutter is the ideal back-to-school gadget
results.author: Ankit Banerjee
results.content:
From design to peel-ready sticker in a single go, the Liene PixCut S1 all-in-one printer and cutter is the ideal back-to-school gadget
Aug 21, 2026 — 5:10 AM ET
Back-to-school usually means two things: a shopping list and things that need labels and stickers. Whether you’re looking to add name tags to your or your kids’ supplies, make planner stickers, or want to add a personalized touch to your laptop lid or dorm room, it can be quite a time-consuming project. Creating a custom sticker sheet typically means designing on one screen, printing on another device, then carrying that sheet to a separate cutter to trace and slice by hand. And any misstep along the way means going right back to the start.
The Liene PixCut S1 is the company’s attempt to combine that entire chain into a single device. Liene has spent 700 days developing, testing, and refining its all-in-one printer and cutter, just in time for the start of the new school year. With the PixCut S1 Starter Kit, you have the perfect tool for making name labels, planner stickers, locker decor, and more. Here’s what you need to know.
What the PixCut S1 does
The main idea behind the PixCut S1 is also its biggest USP: it’s an all-in-one printer and cutter. Liene started the project in July 2023 and spent the following months on product design, finalizing it in March 2024, before any manufacturing even began. That upfront design phase ensured there weren’t any hardware design issues that often accompany a new gadget build. This long development cycle supports the “700 Days Proven, Perfect From Day 1” tagline the brand built around.
It’s definitely worth emphasizing how important the “all-in-one” phrasing is here. Some print-and-cut setups still require you to feed a printed sheet into a second machine and manually align everything perfectly. Liene doesn’t keep it vague or use the phrase loosely. The PixCut S1 keeps the paper in one machine from the first print pass through the final cut, with no manual transfer steps or unnecessary intervention in between.
Everything starts in the Liene Photo app, where you can pick from more than 10,000 templates and creative assets, or upload your own JPG, PNG, or HEIC images. Say you want a sheet of name labels for your first grader’s school supplies. You can use a preset template, drop in a photo, or ask your kids to choose their favorite color scheme, then make several copies of the design on one sheet before sending it to print. If you want to turn your own photos into stickers, you can also use the app’s AI-powered image recognition feature to remove the background.
The app then automatically generates the cut path. Instead of manually tracing an outline, the software detects the shape of the design and sends that path to the machine. If you’ve used any cutting software before, you know that this step is the one that normally takes a while and often requires a lot of trial-and-error. Here, the app removes the background and calculates the outline perfectly, so you don’t have to worry about slightly off cuts or a noticeable border around the stickers. Most importantly, you don’t need manual alignment or tracing.
The PixCut S1 then prints the image using dye-sublimation, adds a protective overcoat in the same print pass, aligns the sheet through built-in sensing, and follows the detected contour to cut it out. What you end up with is a finished, ready-to-peel sticker sheet. So going back to that sheet of name labels, the full sheet comes out already cut and ready to peel apart.
The printing tech behind the PixCut S1
The PixCut S1 uses a 300 x 300 dpi dye-sublimation system built around a 1,280-dot thermal print head, with each element capable of 256 tonal levels. Instead of spraying liquid ink through nozzles that can clog, the process transfers yellow, magenta, and cyan dye layers onto the paper in sequence, then finishes with a clear protective coat.
This results in smoother color gradients and finer detail than a standard inkjet, and you won’t face any of the maintenance issues that come with ink cartridges. Color accuracy was the area Liene’s engineering team spent the most time refining during the 700-day process. And when you see the final product, you’ll notice how everything from prints of family photos and pet portraits to name labels and customized stickers closely matches the original image.
Each print takes about 59 seconds, and the paper cassette holds up to 36 sheets. With this speed and capacity, the PixCut S1 also works for small-batch commercial use, like an Etsy seller printing a set of 10-15 branded labels or custom stickers for an order.
Longevity is also a focus here. Inkjet prints can smear or fade when they get wet or scratched. On the other hand, dye-sublimation bonds the color into the paper’s coating, and the protective overcoat adds another layer of resistance. Some stickers you create need to survive months of wear and tear on a backpack, a water bottle, a laptop lid, or a locker door, and these prints are made to last.
Sleek and compact, and at home on any desk
A traditional home setup, especially one built to handle multiple paper sizes and a full-size ink or toner system, tends to take up a lot of space. And there’s usually a separate cutting machine, too. Meanwhile, the PixCut S1 saves you a ton of desk space, not only because it’s all-in-one, but also because of how sleek and compact it is.
At 281 x 196 x 104.5mm and 2.9 kg, PixCut S1 is roughly 70% smaller than a traditional home printer setup. It’s light enough to move comfortably between a closet shelf and a desk when it’s not in use, and small enough to fit on a craft table, a dorm-room desk, or a kitchen counter. To fit a printer, a laminator, and a cutter into one small chassis, the team made the device’s mechanical design another primary engineering focus during the 700-day process.
Design from a phone, a tablet, or a computer
The Liene Photo app runs on iOS and Android phones, iPads and Android tablets, and laptops and desktops running Windows 10 or later or macOS Monterey 12 or later. A student can pull up the app on their phone between classes to quickly design a set of laptop stickers, while a parent might prefer sitting down with a tablet or laptop on the kitchen table in the evening to get all their kids’ lunchbox, water bottle, and notebook labels ready to go before school starts.
The cross-platform availability is crucial, of course, since different projects require different amounts of screen space. Arranging multiple elements on one sheet, mixing text with images, or fine-tuning sizes and spacing are much easier on a laptop or tablet than a phone. On the other hand, a student decorating a water bottle or locker door between classes just needs their phone.
The PixCut S1 connects over Bluetooth 5.0, and the Starter Kit ships with two paper types: 4 x 7-inch sticker paper and 4 x 6-inch photo paper, with 18 sheets of each included. That covers everything the device is built for, whether you’re designing and cutting custom stickers or printing standalone photos.
Get the Liene PixCut S1 now
The start of the new school year is just around the corner, and the PixCut S1 is primed to jump into action. Name labels for supplies, planner stickers, class schedules, bookmarks, teacher thank-you cards, lunchbox and water bottle labels, locker or dorm decor, laptop decorations, and more – all of it can move through the same machine, from screen to finished product. Liene also extends its support for the education community through ongoing Education Savings, offering students and teachers 15% off eligible purchases.
That’s the idea behind Liene’s “Make Your Ideas Stick” campaign, letting you quickly turn a design into something a kid is excited to peel off and use. Liene has backed up the “700 Days Proven” side of things as well, with features like the printer’s size and color accuracy showcasing the company’s engineering capabilities. A September 2024 crowdfunding campaign drew more than 3,330 backers and over $1 million in preorders before the product reached mass production in January 2025, and Liene says its community has now grown past 75,000 users.
The PixCut S1 Starter Kit includes the machine, plus 18 sheets each of 4 x 7-inch sticker paper and 4 x 6-inch photo paper. From August 24 through August 30, 2026, Liene’s Back-to-School promotion brings the price down to $237.99, a $42 discount off the regular $279.99.
